Option 2 — Invest in marketing and online customer service: Spend £30,000 on social media marketing and a new website with live chat support. Hire 2 customer service agents (£22,000 each/year). Offer a no-questions-asked returns policy to rebuild trust. Keep current production and stock control methods unchanged.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on SnapCase’s ability to improve customer satisfaction. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Introduce TQM and switch to JIT:

An advantage of introducing TQM and JIT is that it directly tackles the root cause of SnapCase’s falling customer satisfaction — printing defects. Currently, several batches have had defects, causing reviews to fall from 4.5/5 to 3.6/5. TQM would train all 35 staff to check quality at every stage of production, catching defects before cases are shipped. This is because TQM aims to prevent mistakes rather than finding them after production. This means that customers would receive consistently high-quality phone cases without printing errors. As a result, customer complaints would fall, returns would decrease, and reviews should improve back towards 4.5+/5. Therefore, TQM addresses the fundamental problem — the product itself — rather than just managing perceptions. Switching to JIT from the local supplier (£2,800/month warehouse savings) would also free up cash to fund the £15,000 TQM training. However, this depends on whether all 35 staff buy into the TQM culture change, as TQM requires every employee to take personal responsibility.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Invest in marketing and online customer service:

An advantage of investing in marketing and customer service is that it directly addresses how customers perceive SnapCase. The £30,000 social media spend would increase brand visibility and attract new customers, while the live chat and no-questions-asked returns policy would make existing customers feel supported. This is because modern consumers expect fast, accessible customer service online, and a generous returns policy reduces the perceived risk of buying. This means that even if some defective cases still reach customers, the easy returns process would limit frustration. As a result, SnapCase’s online reputation could improve as customers share positive experiences of the returns process and responsive live chat. Therefore, better customer service could win back trust in the short term. However, this depends on whether managing perceptions is enough when the underlying quality problem remains — no-questions-asked returns would cost SnapCase money on every defective case returned, and customers who repeatedly receive faulty products will eventually stop buying regardless of how easy returns are.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 1 (TQM and JIT) will have the biggest impact on SnapCase’s ability to improve customer satisfaction. Although marketing and returns policies would help manage the short-term damage to SnapCase’s reputation, this is outweighed by the fact that Option 2 does not fix the actual problem — defective phone cases are still being produced. No amount of marketing can overcome a product that keeps arriving with printing errors. However, this depends on whether the TQM training is thorough enough to change the production culture across all 35 staff. The most important factor is that customer satisfaction is ultimately driven by product quality — if customers receive a perfect phone case every time, they do not need a generous returns policy or live chat support. In the long term, TQM would reduce returns, lower costs, improve reviews, and build the kind of consistent reputation that attracts loyal, repeat customers. The £9,600 per year saved from eliminating the warehouse (JIT) would more than cover the £15,000 one-off TQM training cost. Therefore, Option 1 is the best way to improve customer satisfaction because it eliminates the root cause of the problem rather than treating the symptoms.

questions.caseStudy: BrightStar Tutoring is a small business that provides one-to-one maths and English tutoring. The owner, Anisha, manages all 14 tutors herself with no managers between them — a completely flat structure. Tutors work on zero-hours contracts. Two experienced tutors have recently left because they felt Anisha’s autocratic management style did not value their ideas for new courses. Customer complaints have risen 30% since they left.
questions.question: Analyse TWO drawbacks of Anisha’s management approach at BrightStar Tutoring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Drawback 1 — Autocratic style causes staff to leave: One drawback is that Anisha’s autocratic management style has directly caused two experienced tutors to resign because they felt their ideas for new courses were not valued. BrightStar only has 14 tutors, so losing two represents a significant loss of expertise. This means that BrightStar has lost experienced staff who were delivering high-quality tutoring. As a result, customer complaints have risen 30% since they left, suggesting the remaining tutors cannot fully replace the quality those experienced tutors provided. Therefore, Anisha’s refusal to listen to ideas has damaged both her workforce and her customer satisfaction. This could lead to further customer losses if complaints continue to rise.

Drawback 2 — Flat structure with wide span is unmanageable: A second drawback is that Anisha manages all 14 tutors directly with no middle managers, giving her a very wide span of control. This means she cannot give each tutor adequate supervision, feedback or support. As a result, quality may be inconsistent across tutors, which explains the 30% rise in customer complaints. Therefore, the combination of autocratic management and an overly wide span of control means tutors are unsupervised AND unable to contribute ideas — the worst of both worlds for motivation and quality.

questions.caseStudy: Swift Logistics Ltd operates a fleet of 40 delivery vans across the Midlands. It employs 55 drivers. Staff turnover is 35% per year — well above the industry average of 18%. Exit interviews show that drivers leave because of low wages (£9.50/hr vs the industry average of £11.20/hr) and a lack of training. New drivers currently receive a 1-page leaflet on their first day instead of formal induction training. Last month, a new driver damaged a customer’s property because they had not been shown the correct unloading procedure.
questions.question: Analyse TWO benefits for Swift Logistics of improving its training programme.
questions.modelAnswer:
Benefit 1 — Reduced mistakes and damage: One benefit of improving training is that it would prevent costly incidents like the recent property damage caused by an untrained new driver. Currently, new drivers receive only a 1-page leaflet instead of proper induction training. A formal programme teaching correct unloading procedures would mean drivers know exactly how to handle deliveries safely from day one. As a result, Swift Logistics would avoid compensation claims and reputational damage. Therefore, the cost of training is far less than the cost of ongoing mistakes and insurance claims.

Benefit 2 — Reduced staff turnover: A second benefit is that better training would help reduce Swift’s 35% staff turnover rate, nearly double the industry average of 18%. Exit interviews show lack of training is a key reason drivers leave. Investing in induction and ongoing skills development would make drivers feel valued and more competent. As a result, more drivers would stay, reducing the constant cycle of recruitment and training costs. Therefore, improved training directly addresses one of the two main reasons for Swift’s high turnover.

questions.caseStudy: VintageVault is a private limited company selling vintage clothing online. It has grown from 5 to 38 employees in two years. The founder, Kai, still makes every decision personally — from choosing stock to approving social media posts. Kai’s span of control is 38. Orders are often delayed because Kai is too busy to approve them. Two senior buyers have threatened to resign because Kai ignores their recommendations on which items to stock.
questions.question: Analyse TWO ways VintageVault might benefit from creating a taller organisational structure with middle managers.
questions.modelAnswer:
Benefit 1 — Kai’s span of control becomes manageable: One benefit of adding middle managers is that Kai’s span of control would drop from 38 to perhaps 3–4 managers, who each oversee their own team. Currently, orders are delayed because Kai is too busy to approve them. This means that middle managers could handle day-to-day decisions in their areas, freeing Kai to focus on strategy. As a result, orders would be processed faster and customer satisfaction would improve. Therefore, a taller structure removes the bottleneck that is currently causing delayed orders.

Benefit 2 — Improved staff retention: A second benefit is that middle managers could listen to and act on the recommendations of the two senior buyers who are threatening to resign. Currently, Kai ignores their stock recommendations. A buying manager role would give them someone who values their expertise. As a result, senior buyers would feel valued and are more likely to stay. Therefore, the taller structure protects VintageVault from losing its most knowledgeable employees.

questions.caseStudy: PeakFit Gym has 12 personal trainers. Staff turnover is low and trainers are highly experienced. A new gym has opened nearby offering classes with the latest celebrity fitness trends. PeakFit’s owner is considering two options: (1) Send 4 trainers on an expensive 3-month off-the-job course (£4,500 per trainer) at a specialist fitness academy to learn the latest techniques, or (2) Hire one new trainer who already has these skills on a £35,000 salary (external recruitment) and have them train the existing team on-the-job. The off-the-job course runs during PeakFit’s busiest period.
questions.question: Recommend whether PeakFit should choose off-the-job training (Option 1) or hire a new trainer (Option 2). Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR Option 2 (hire new trainer):

An advantage of hiring a new trainer is that PeakFit immediately gains the latest fitness skills without taking existing trainers away from their clients. The off-the-job course would remove 4 trainers for 3 months during PeakFit’s busiest period, directly reducing the gym’s capacity to serve members. This is because each absent trainer would cancel client sessions, leading to lost revenue and frustrated members who may switch to the new competitor. This means that hiring one new trainer at £35,000 avoids this disruption entirely — existing trainers continue serving clients while the new hire teaches them the latest techniques on-the-job. As a result, PeakFit responds to the competitive threat without losing any revenue during the transition. Therefore, external recruitment is a faster and less disruptive way to acquire new skills. This depends on whether the new trainer is able to effectively teach existing staff while also building their own client base.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, a more balanced view would consider that on-the-job training from one new hire may not be as thorough as a specialist 3-month course at a fitness academy. It also depends on whether the new trainer fits PeakFit’s culture — existing staff have low turnover and are highly experienced, so a new person must earn their respect. Furthermore, the £35,000 annual salary is an ongoing cost, whereas the £18,000 training cost (4 × £4,500) is a one-off investment that permanently upskills 4 trainers.

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend PeakFit should choose Option 2 — hire the new trainer. In the short term, this avoids losing 4 trainers during the busiest period, protecting revenue at a critical time when a new competitor has just opened. The most important factor is timing — PeakFit needs to respond immediately, and waiting 3 months for off-the-job training is too slow. The new hire can begin teaching existing staff on-the-job straight away while also serving their own clients. Therefore, Option 2 is the better choice because it responds to the competitive threat faster and without revenue loss.

questions.caseStudy: GlowUp Hair Salon employs 8 stylists. The owner, Fatima, uses an autocratic management style — she makes all decisions about services, prices and scheduling. Senior stylist Maya has asked Fatima to adopt a democratic approach, allowing stylists to suggest new treatments and set their own schedules. Maya argues this would reduce staff turnover (currently 25% per year) and attract new customers. However, Fatima is worried that inconsistent decisions could damage GlowUp’s brand. GlowUp’s customer satisfaction rating is 4.2/5 — competitors average 4.6/5. Three stylists have left in the past year citing ‘feeling undervalued’.
questions.question: Recommend whether Fatima should change from an autocratic to a democratic management style. Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR changing to democratic:

An advantage of changing to a democratic management style is that it would directly address the reason stylists are leaving. Three stylists left in the past year citing ‘feeling undervalued’, and the current 25% staff turnover is costly. This is because a democratic approach would involve stylists in decisions about new treatments and scheduling, making them feel their opinions matter. This means that staff like Maya would feel valued and are more likely to stay, reducing turnover. As a result, GlowUp saves on recruitment and training costs while retaining experienced stylists. Therefore, a democratic style could improve both staff retention and customer satisfaction — currently 4.2/5 vs competitors’ 4.6/5. This depends on whether Fatima can genuinely share decision-making after years of making every decision herself.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, a more balanced view recognises that Fatima’s concern about inconsistent decisions has merit. If 8 stylists each set their own schedules and suggest different treatments, GlowUp could lose its cohesive brand identity. It also depends on whether democratic decision-making slows things down — consulting 8 people on every decision takes time, and some decisions (pricing, branding) may need to remain centralised.

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend that Fatima should move towards a democratic style, but gradually rather than all at once. In the short term, she should consult stylists on new treatments and scheduling while keeping pricing and branding decisions centralised. The most important factor is that 3 stylists have already left and GlowUp’s satisfaction (4.2/5) trails competitors (4.6/5) — doing nothing will make both problems worse. Therefore, a gradual shift to democratic management is the best way to retain staff and close the satisfaction gap.

questions.caseStudy: MapleCraft Furniture makes bespoke dining tables. It has grown from 8 to 32 employees in 3 years. The founder, Liam, still manages everyone directly (span of control: 32). Communication problems are increasing — two large orders were shipped late last month because Liam forgot to pass on customer specifications. Three skilled carpenters have left, saying they felt ‘invisible’ in such a large team. Option 1 — Create a taller structure: Add 3 team leaders (production, sales, quality) at £32,000 each/year. Liam’s span of control drops from 32 to 3. Team leaders manage 8–12 employees each. Total additional cost: £96,000/year. Option 2 — Decentralise and delegate: Keep the flat structure but give 4 senior employees authority to make decisions in their areas (production scheduling, quality checks, customer orders, procurement). Offer them a £3,000 pay rise each (£12,000 total). No new hires needed. Liam keeps a wide span but shares decision-making.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on MapleCraft’s ability to improve communication and retain employees. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Create a taller structure:

An advantage of creating a taller structure with 3 team leaders is that it directly solves MapleCraft’s communication problems. Currently, Liam manages all 32 employees with a span of control of 32, and two large orders were shipped late because he forgot to pass on customer specifications. Adding team leaders for production, sales and quality would mean each leader manages 8–12 employees and takes responsibility for communication within their team. This is because team leaders would receive customer specifications directly and pass them to the right workers, eliminating the risk of Liam forgetting or being overwhelmed. This means that orders are processed accurately and on time. As a result, late deliveries would be avoided and customer trust maintained. Therefore, a taller structure eliminates the single point of failure. However, this depends on whether £96,000 per year in additional salaries is affordable and whether Liam is willing to genuinely delegate authority.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Decentralise and delegate:

An advantage of decentralisation is that it costs far less — £12,000 per year vs £96,000 — while still addressing the core problem. Giving 4 senior employees authority over production scheduling, quality, customer orders and procurement means decisions are made faster by people closest to the work. This is because senior employees already understand the processes and have the skills to make good decisions. This means that Liam no longer needs to personally approve every specification and order. As a result, the bottleneck that caused late deliveries is removed. Therefore, decentralisation offers a cost-effective solution. However, this depends on whether the 4 employees are willing to take on extra responsibility for only £3,000 extra, and Liam still has an unsustainably wide span of control.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 1 (taller structure) will have the biggest impact on improving communication and retaining employees. Although decentralisation is much cheaper (£12,000 vs £96,000), this is outweighed by the fact that it does not solve the retention problem — three skilled carpenters left because they felt ‘invisible’ in a team of 32, and delegating to 4 senior employees does not reduce team sizes or create the closer management relationships that would make employees feel valued. Team leaders managing 8–12 people can build personal relationships and provide regular feedback. However, this depends on whether Liam can afford £96,000 and is willing to step back. The most important factor is that MapleCraft is a bespoke furniture business where skilled carpenters are extremely difficult to replace — losing more staff would be far more costly than £96,000 in team leader salaries. Therefore, Option 1 addresses both problems simultaneously — communication AND retention.

questions.caseStudy: TechTalent is a recruitment agency with 20 consultants. It places IT professionals in jobs across the UK. Consultants currently earn a basic salary of £24,000 plus 10% commission on placement fees. Staff turnover is 40% per year — the highest in the industry (average: 22%). Exit interviews reveal two main reasons for leaving: (1) consultants feel the commission structure is unfair because experienced staff get the best client accounts, and (2) there is no formal training — new recruits are expected to ‘learn by watching’. Option 1 — Change the reward structure: Replace individual commission with team-based profit sharing (15% of profits shared equally). Increase basic salary from £24,000 to £28,000. Total estimated additional cost: £115,000/year. Option 2 — Invest in a formal training programme: Introduce a 2-week induction for new starters plus ongoing off-the-job training (1 day per month at a specialist recruitment academy). Cost: £2,500 per employee per year (£50,000 total). New starters paired with a mentor for first 6 months.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on TechTalent’s ability to reduce staff turnover. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Change the reward structure:

An advantage of changing the reward structure is that it directly addresses the main reason consultants leave — perceived unfairness of the commission system. Exit interviews show experienced staff get the best client accounts, meaning newer consultants earn less regardless of effort. Replacing individual commission with team-based profit sharing (15% shared equally) and raising basic salary from £24,000 to £28,000 removes this inequality. This is because all consultants benefit equally from the company’s success. This means that newer consultants feel the system is fair and are motivated to stay. As a result, TechTalent’s 40% turnover could fall significantly. Therefore, a fairer reward system tackles the root cause. However, this depends on whether experienced consultants accept losing their individual commission advantage.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Invest in formal training:

An advantage of investing in training is that it directly addresses the second main reason for leaving — the lack of any formal support. Currently, new starters are expected to ‘learn by watching’ with no structured programme, which is demotivating and ineffective. A 2-week induction plus monthly off-the-job training at a specialist academy would give new consultants skills and confidence. This is because structured training with a mentor means new recruits develop competence faster. This means they are more likely to make successful placements early, earning commission and building confidence. As a result, the frustration that drives new recruits to leave would be reduced. Therefore, training attacks turnover at its source. However, this depends on whether £50,000 per year is sufficient and whether consultants are willing to give up 1 day per month.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 1 (changing the reward structure) will have the biggest impact on reducing staff turnover. Although training addresses an important secondary issue, this is outweighed by the fact that the commission system is identified as the PRIMARY reason consultants leave. However, this depends on whether top performers accept the change. The most important factor is that at 40% turnover, TechTalent replaces 8 of its 20 consultants every year — the cost of constantly recruiting replacements (typically £5,000–£8,000 per new hire) almost certainly exceeds the £115,000 cost of the new reward structure. In the long term, TechTalent should implement BOTH options — but fixing the reward structure first will retain more consultants immediately, creating the stable workforce that training can then develop. Therefore, Option 1 will have the biggest impact because it removes the unfairness that drives the majority of leavers out the door.

questions.caseStudy: ZenBrew is a small coffee roastery that sells premium coffee beans online. It has been growing steadily for 2 years. Its main competitor has just launched a major TV advertising campaign. ZenBrew cannot afford TV advertising but has 12,000 Instagram followers. The owner is considering running a social media competition where customers share photos of their ZenBrew coffee for a chance to win a year’s free supply. ZenBrew’s USP is that every bag is hand-roasted and includes a personal note from the roaster.
questions.question: Analyse TWO benefits for ZenBrew of using social media to promote its coffee.
questions.modelAnswer:
Benefit 1 — Cost-effective reach: One benefit is that social media is free to use and ZenBrew already has 12,000 Instagram followers. ZenBrew cannot afford TV advertising, but a social media competition costs almost nothing to run. This means ZenBrew can promote its products to thousands of potential customers without the enormous expense of a TV campaign. As a result, the competition could generate significant brand awareness within ZenBrew’s budget. Therefore, social media allows ZenBrew to compete with its rival’s TV campaign without matching its spending.

Benefit 2 — User-generated content builds authenticity: A second benefit is that the photo competition creates user-generated content that acts as free promotion. Customers sharing photos of their ZenBrew coffee on their own Instagram accounts exposes the brand to their followers. This means ZenBrew reaches new audiences through personal recommendations, which customers trust more than paid advertising. As a result, each competition entry becomes a mini-advert seen by the entrant’s friends and followers. Therefore, the competition could grow ZenBrew’s customer base organically, building the authentic, personal brand image that matches its USP of hand-roasted coffee with personal notes.

questions.caseStudy: FreshFit Meals delivers healthy recipe boxes to customers across the UK. It has been using price penetration — charging £4.99 per meal (competitors charge £7–£9). FreshFit has built a customer base of 8,000 subscribers in 18 months. The owner now wants to raise prices to £7.49 per meal to improve profit margins. Customer research shows 35% of subscribers say they chose FreshFit mainly because of the low price. FreshFit’s food quality ratings are 4.6/5.
questions.question: Analyse TWO risks for FreshFit of increasing its prices from £4.99 to £7.49 per meal.
questions.modelAnswer:
Risk 1 — Losing price-sensitive customers: One risk is that 35% of subscribers say they chose FreshFit mainly because of the low price. Raising from £4.99 to £7.49 is a 50% increase. This means that over a third of FreshFit’s 8,000 customers could cancel their subscriptions because the product is no longer the cheapest option. As a result, FreshFit could lose approximately 2,800 subscribers (35% of 8,000), significantly reducing revenue. Therefore, the price increase could harm FreshFit more than it helps if the lost customers are not replaced.

Risk 2 — Entering a competitive price range: A second risk is that the new price of £7.49 falls within the competitor range of £7–£9. At £4.99, FreshFit was clearly the cheapest option. At £7.49, it is just another mid-price option competing directly with established rivals. This means FreshFit loses its price-based USP without having built a strong enough brand to justify the higher price. As a result, customers may switch to better-known competitors at a similar price. Therefore, the price increase removes the competitive advantage that attracted customers in the first place.

questions.caseStudy: GlowSkin Cosmetics sells skincare products through 3 high street shops. Online competitors have been growing rapidly. GlowSkin’s owner is considering adding e-commerce to sell products through a new website. Setting up the website would cost £8,000. GlowSkin’s products are popular because customers can test them in-store before buying. 72% of customers say they prefer to try products before purchasing. Monthly shop rent across all 3 stores: £4,500.
questions.question: Analyse TWO drawbacks for GlowSkin of selling its products through e-commerce.
questions.modelAnswer:
Drawback 1 — Customers cannot test products: One drawback is that 72% of GlowSkin’s customers say they prefer to try products before purchasing. Skincare is a sensory product — customers want to feel the texture, smell the product and test it on their skin. E-commerce removes this entirely. This means that online customers may be reluctant to buy without trying, leading to lower conversion rates. As a result, GlowSkin may invest £8,000 in a website that generates fewer sales than expected. Therefore, e-commerce may not suit a product where the in-store experience is the key reason customers buy.

Drawback 2 — Higher returns: A second drawback is that customers buying skincare online without testing may be more likely to return products if they don’t like the scent, texture or effect. In physical shops, customers test before buying so returns are rare. This means GlowSkin faces higher return rates, postage costs for returns, and potential waste from opened products that cannot be resold. As a result, the actual profit from online sales could be significantly lower than expected. Therefore, e-commerce may increase revenue but reduce profitability once returns and delivery costs are factored in.

questions.caseStudy: PeakView makes outdoor jackets and sells them through its own website and 6 independent retailers. Sales have been flat for 12 months. The owner is considering two options: (1) Use price penetration — reduce prices by 30% to attract new customers and increase market share. Current price: £120 per jacket. Cost per jacket: £65. Monthly sales: 400 jackets. (2) Sponsor a popular hiking YouTuber (250,000 subscribers) for £15,000 per year to promote PeakView products. The YouTuber’s audience matches PeakView’s target market of outdoor enthusiasts aged 25–45.
questions.question: Recommend whether PeakView should reduce prices (Option 1) or use sponsorship (Option 2) to increase sales. Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR Option 2 (sponsorship):

An advantage of sponsoring the hiking YouTuber is that PeakView would reach 250,000 subscribers who are exactly its target market — outdoor enthusiasts aged 25–45. A 30% price reduction (Option 1) would cut the price from £120 to £84, reducing the profit per jacket from £55 to just £19. This is because sponsorship builds brand awareness and credibility without destroying profit margins. This means PeakView can attract new customers through a trusted recommendation while maintaining its £120 price point and £55 profit per jacket. As a result, each new customer acquired through sponsorship is worth nearly three times more than a customer acquired through the discounted price. Therefore, sponsorship is a more sustainable way to grow sales. This depends on whether the YouTuber’s followers actually convert into paying customers.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, a more balanced view would consider that the sponsorship costs £15,000 per year with no guarantee of increased sales. The YouTuber’s subscribers may watch the content but never buy a £120 jacket. It also depends on whether PeakView’s flat sales are caused by lack of awareness (which sponsorship fixes) or by the price being too high compared to competitors (which only a price reduction fixes).

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend PeakView should choose Option 2 — sponsorship. In the short term, £15,000 is a manageable investment, whereas a 30% price cut would immediately slash profit per jacket from £55 to £19 on ALL 400 monthly sales. The most important factor is that PeakView’s cost per jacket is £65 — a 30% price cut leaves only £19 profit, meaning PeakView would need to nearly triple sales volume just to maintain the same total profit. Sponsorship grows the brand without damaging margins. Therefore, sponsorship is the better option because it builds long-term brand awareness while protecting profitability.

questions.caseStudy: BiteBox makes healthy protein bars. It currently sells exclusively through a wholesaler who distributes to 200 shops nationwide. BiteBox receives £1.20 per bar from the wholesaler (the wholesaler sells to shops for £1.80, shops sell for £2.99). BiteBox’s production cost is £0.75 per bar. Monthly output: 50,000 bars. BiteBox is considering switching to selling directly to customers through its own e-commerce website at £2.49 per bar (including free delivery). The website would cost £6,000 to build. Delivery costs: £0.40 per bar. The wholesaler has warned that if BiteBox sells direct, the wholesaler will stop stocking BiteBox products.
questions.question: Recommend whether BiteBox should start selling directly through e-commerce. Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR e-commerce:

An advantage of selling directly through e-commerce is that BiteBox would earn £2.49 per bar minus £0.75 production and £0.40 delivery = £1.34 profit per bar, compared to only £0.45 per bar through the wholesaler (£1.20 – £0.75). This is because cutting out the wholesaler removes the middleman’s margin, allowing BiteBox to keep a much larger share of each sale. This means that BiteBox’s profit per bar almost triples. As a result, BiteBox could potentially earn far more from fewer direct sales than from 50,000 bars through the wholesaler. Therefore, e-commerce could dramatically improve BiteBox’s profitability. This depends on whether BiteBox can attract enough direct customers to replace the wholesale volume.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, the wholesaler has warned it will stop stocking BiteBox if it sells direct. This means BiteBox could lose access to 200 shops overnight — 50,000 bars per month of guaranteed sales. Building an e-commerce customer base from scratch takes months or years, and during that time BiteBox may have no revenue at all. It also depends on whether BiteBox can handle its own marketing, packaging and delivery logistics, which the wholesaler currently does.

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend BiteBox should NOT switch to e-commerce exclusively. Although the profit per bar is much higher, this is outweighed by the risk of losing 50,000 monthly sales overnight with no replacement customers. The most important factor is that the wholesaler provides guaranteed, immediate volume — losing this before the website has built a customer base could bankrupt BiteBox. A better approach is to keep the wholesaler relationship AND quietly launch the website to test direct-to-consumer demand, only scaling back wholesale once online sales are proven. Therefore, BiteBox should use e-commerce as an additional channel, not a replacement.

questions.caseStudy: VitalFit manufactures and sells two products: an exercise bike (launched 5 years ago) and a rowing machine (launched 6 months ago). The exercise bike has the largest UK market share but the market has stopped growing. The rowing machine has low market share but the rowing machine market is growing by 25% per year. Option 1 — Use TV advertising during Premier League matches to promote the exercise bike in the UK. A single prime-time slot costs £35,000. Previous billboard campaigns failed to meet sales targets. Over 2 million viewers per match. Option 2 — Add a touchscreen to the rowing machine with live-streamed workout classes (monthly subscription: £12). This would create a USP and allow VitalFit to enter international markets. Development cost: £80,000. The touchscreen would increase the rowing machine’s price by 30%.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on VitalFit’s revenue. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: TV advertising for exercise bike:

An advantage of TV advertising is that VitalFit could reach over 2 million viewers during Premier League matches, generating massive brand awareness. Previous billboard campaigns failed to meet sales targets, and TV allows VitalFit to demonstrate the exercise bike in action. This is because TV is far more persuasive than a static billboard — viewers can see the product being used, which builds desire. This means VitalFit may reach its target market of fitness enthusiasts more effectively. As a result, a successful campaign could significantly increase UK sales of the exercise bike. Therefore, TV advertising could boost short-term revenue. However, this depends on whether the exercise bike market is growing — the data says it is NOT growing, which means TV advertising is investing in a product with limited upside. Even with 2 million viewers, the market itself is stagnant.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Touchscreen rowing machine for global market:

An advantage of the touchscreen is that VitalFit would create a unique product with a strong USP in the fast-growing rowing machine market (25% annual growth). The £12 monthly subscription creates recurring revenue — every customer pays £144 per year on top of the purchase price. This is because subscription revenue compounds over time, meaning each customer becomes increasingly valuable. This means that even though the 30% price increase narrows the potential market, the subscription revenue more than compensates per customer. As a result, entering international markets with a differentiated product opens up a far larger opportunity than the UK exercise bike market alone. Therefore, the touchscreen creates both immediate sales and long-term recurring income. However, this depends on whether the £80,000 development cost is affordable and whether international customers will pay the higher price.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 2 (touchscreen rowing machine) will have the biggest impact on VitalFit’s revenue. Although TV advertising would reach 2 million UK viewers, this is outweighed by the fact that the exercise bike market has stopped growing — VitalFit would be advertising a cash cow in a stagnant market. The rowing machine market is growing by 25% per year, meaning the opportunity is far larger. However, this depends on whether the development costs can be managed alongside normal operations. The most important factor is that the subscription model (£12/month) creates recurring revenue that grows with every customer — something TV advertising for a one-off purchase cannot match. In the long term, international expansion with a differentiated, subscription-based product is a far stronger growth strategy than promoting an existing product in a flat UK market. Therefore, Option 2 will have the biggest impact because it targets growth, creates recurring revenue, and positions VitalFit for international success.

questions.caseStudy: CoastalBrew makes artisan ice cream and sells it from one shop in a seaside town. Summer sales (June–Aug) are very strong but winter sales (Oct–Feb) are almost zero. Annual revenue: £95,000 (80% earned in summer). 4 employees. Option 1 — Supply a local restaurant chain. The chain has 6 restaurants across the region. It would add CoastalBrew’s logo to its dessert menu (free promotion). CoastalBrew would receive 50% of the menu price. The chain offers a 4-week trial. Option 2 — Launch an e-commerce delivery service for nationwide online orders. Website cost: £5,500. Insulated packaging per order: £4.50. Minimum order value: £25. CoastalBrew would keep 100% of revenue. However, ice cream delivery requires specialist cold-chain logistics and 8% of deliveries in similar businesses arrive damaged.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on CoastalBrew’s ability to increase winter sales. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Supply the restaurant chain:

An advantage of supplying the restaurant chain is that CoastalBrew immediately gains access to 6 restaurants and their existing customer base. The restaurant will add CoastalBrew’s logo to its dessert menu, providing free promotion to every diner. CoastalBrew receives 50% of the menu price, and the chain offers a 4-week trial to test demand. This is because CoastalBrew does not need to attract its own customers — the restaurant already has diners who will see the desserts on the menu. This means CoastalBrew gains winter sales without the cost of marketing, packaging or delivery logistics. As a result, revenue increases during the October–February period when the seaside shop earns almost nothing. Therefore, the restaurant partnership provides low-risk, low-cost winter revenue. However, this depends on whether receiving only 50% of the menu price generates enough revenue to justify production costs and delivery to 6 locations.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: E-commerce delivery nationwide:

An advantage of e-commerce is that CoastalBrew keeps 100% of revenue and reaches customers nationwide, not just locally. The minimum order of £25 ensures each delivery is worthwhile. This is because e-commerce removes geographic limitations — customers across the UK can order artisan ice cream year-round. This means the potential market is enormously larger than 6 local restaurants. As a result, if demand is strong, e-commerce revenue could far exceed what the restaurant chain provides. Therefore, e-commerce offers higher revenue potential per sale. However, this depends on whether customers will order ice cream online in winter, whether the £4.50 insulated packaging costs make orders profitable, and whether the 8% damage rate destroys customer trust.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 1 (restaurant chain) will have the biggest impact on CoastalBrew’s winter sales. Although e-commerce reaches a larger market, this is outweighed by the fact that ice cream delivery is logistically difficult — 8% of deliveries arriving damaged would create complaints, refunds and reputational damage for a small business with only 4 employees. The restaurant partnership, by contrast, is low-risk: the 4-week trial tests demand before any long-term commitment, the restaurant handles serving to customers, and the logo on the menu is free advertising. However, this depends on whether 50% of the menu price covers CoastalBrew’s production and delivery costs. The most important factor is that CoastalBrew has only 4 employees — managing a nationwide e-commerce delivery operation with cold-chain logistics is an enormous operational challenge for such a small team, whereas supplying 6 restaurants is manageable. In the long term, if the restaurant trial succeeds, CoastalBrew could supply additional restaurant chains across the region. Therefore, Option 1 is the better choice because it matches CoastalBrew’s small size, avoids delivery risks, and generates guaranteed winter revenue through an established customer base.

questions.caseStudy: SwiftServe is a catering business that provides food for corporate events. The business has been growing rapidly — revenue increased from £80,000 to £210,000 in two years. However, the owner, Priya, is struggling with cash flow because most clients pay 60 days after the event. Priya’s overdraft has been used every month for the past 8 months. Interest rates have recently risen from 4% to 7%. Priya is considering switching to a bank loan to pay off the overdraft and using the loan for the next 3 years.
questions.question: Analyse TWO effects of the interest rate rise on SwiftServe’s financial position.
questions.modelAnswer:
Effect 1 — More expensive overdraft: One effect is that SwiftServe’s overdraft costs will increase significantly. Priya has used the overdraft every month for the past 8 months because clients pay 60 days after events. The interest rate has risen from 4% to 7%. This means that the monthly interest charges on the overdraft will increase by 75% (from 4% to 7%), directly reducing the amount of cash available for running the business. As a result, more of SwiftServe’s revenue goes towards interest payments rather than being reinvested. Therefore, the interest rate rise makes SwiftServe’s existing cash flow problem even worse — the business is paying more to borrow money it already cannot avoid borrowing.

Effect 2 — Higher cost of switching to a bank loan: A second effect is that if Priya switches to a bank loan, the interest rate on that loan will also be higher than it would have been before. Priya is considering a 3-year bank loan to pay off the overdraft. At 7%, a £30,000 loan would cost approximately £6,300 in interest over 3 years — compared to £3,600 at the old 4% rate. This means that the total cost of the loan is £2,700 more than it would have been before the rate rise. As a result, whichever source of finance Priya chooses — overdraft or loan — both are now more expensive. Therefore, the interest rate rise increases costs across all of SwiftServe’s borrowing options, squeezing profit margins at a time when the business is already growing fast and needs cash.

questions.caseStudy: NovaTech is an IT consultancy that wants to expand by opening a second office. Cost: £120,000. NovaTech has £85,000 in retained profits. The owners are considering two options: (1) Use retained profits (£85,000) and take a £35,000 bank loan for the remainder. (2) Issue shares to raise the full £120,000 from two new investors.
questions.question: Analyse TWO advantages for NovaTech of using retained profits and a bank loan (Option 1) rather than issuing shares.
questions.modelAnswer:
Advantage 1 — Owners keep full control: One advantage is that using retained profits and a loan means the current owners keep 100% ownership and decision-making power. If NovaTech issued shares, two new investors would own part of the business and expect a say in decisions. This means the owners can continue running the business exactly as they choose without external interference. As a result, the owners’ vision for the second office — location, staffing, services — is protected. Therefore, Option 1 preserves the independence that built NovaTech’s success.

Advantage 2 — Only £35,000 needs repaying: A second advantage is that NovaTech only needs to borrow £35,000 because £85,000 comes from retained profits, which are free (no interest). This means the interest costs are based on £35,000, not £120,000 — a much smaller debt. As a result, monthly repayments are manageable and the total interest paid over the loan period is relatively low. Therefore, combining retained profits with a small loan is the cheapest financing option that still provides all £120,000 needed.

questions.caseStudy: BrightSmile is a dental practice. Revenue: £420,000/year. Cost of sales: £168,000. Total expenses: £189,000. Net profit: £63,000. The practice manager wants to invest £45,000 in a new digital X-ray machine that would generate an additional £72,000 in profit over 6 years. A competitor dental practice in the same town has a net profit margin of 20%.
questions.question: Analyse TWO ways financial data could help BrightSmile make better business decisions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Way 1 — Comparing profit margins against competitors: BrightSmile’s net profit margin is (£63,000 ÷ £420,000) × 100 = 15%. The competitor’s NPM is 20%. This means BrightSmile can see that its costs are proportionally higher than its competitor’s. As a result, the practice manager can investigate where costs are highest and take action — perhaps negotiating better prices on dental supplies or reducing expenses. Therefore, financial data pinpoints underperformance and guides targeted cost reduction.

Way 2 — Evaluating the X-ray machine investment using ARR: The X-ray machine costs £45,000 and generates £72,000 additional profit over 6 years. Average annual profit = £72,000 ÷ 6 = £12,000. ARR = (£12,000 ÷ £45,000) × 100 = 26.7%. This means BrightSmile can see the investment offers a strong 26.7% annual return. As a result, the practice manager can compare this against other uses of the £45,000 (e.g. hiring another dentist, marketing) and make an evidence-based decision. Therefore, ARR provides a clear, numerical basis for comparing investment options.

questions.caseStudy: CloudBase needs 4 new computers costing £28,000. The business has £30,000 in retained profits. The computers are expected to generate an additional £42,000 in profit over 5 years (ARR = 30%). The alternative is to lease the computers at £7,200/year. After 3 years, leased computers can be returned for newer models. Technology changes rapidly in web design. CloudBase’s current computers are 4 years old and frequently crash, causing missed deadlines.
questions.question: Recommend whether CloudBase should use retained profits to purchase the computers or lease them. Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR retained profits:

An advantage of using retained profits is that CloudBase avoids any ongoing payments, keeping the full £42,000 additional profit over 5 years. The ARR is 30%, meaning the investment generates a strong return. CloudBase has £30,000 in retained profits and the computers cost £28,000, so the purchase is affordable. This is because retained profit is free money — no interest, no monthly repayments. This means every penny of additional profit stays in the business. As a result, CloudBase’s financial position strengthens over time. Therefore, purchasing outright maximises the return on investment. This depends on whether spending £28,000 of £30,000 leaves enough cash for emergencies.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, technology changes rapidly in web design. Computers bought today may be outdated within 3 years, but CloudBase would be stuck with them for 5 years. Leasing at £7,200/year allows CloudBase to return computers after 3 years for newer models. It also depends on whether £2,000 remaining in reserves (£30,000 − £28,000) is enough of a safety net for a growing business.

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend CloudBase should use retained profits. Leasing over 5 years would cost £36,000 (£7,200 × 5) — £8,000 MORE than the £28,000 purchase price — and CloudBase would never own the computers. The most important factor is that the current computers are 4 years old and frequently crash, causing missed deadlines. The business needs reliable equipment NOW, and owning it outright is cheaper in total. However, CloudBase should set aside some of the £42,000 additional profit to fund replacements in 3–4 years. Therefore, purchasing is the best option because it maximises profit and solves the immediate reliability problem.

questions.caseStudy: FreshFields Farm Shop wants to expand its online delivery service. It needs £40,000. Option 1: Bank loan at 6% interest over 5 years, secured against the owner’s house. Monthly repayments: £773. Option 2: Sell 40% of the business to a local investor for £40,000. The investor wants a seat on the board and a share of profits. FreshFields currently makes £52,000 net profit per year. The owner, Sam, has built the brand’s reputation for locally sourced, organic produce over 8 years.
questions.question: Recommend whether Sam should use a bank loan or sell shares to fund the expansion. Give reasons for your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Argument FOR bank loan:

An advantage of the bank loan is that Sam keeps 100% ownership and control of FreshFields. The investor wants 40% of the business AND a board seat — meaning Sam loses nearly half the ownership and must share decision-making. This is because a bank loan is repaid in fixed monthly instalments (£773/month), after which Sam owes nothing and still owns everything. This means Sam retains full control over the brand’s direction, sourcing and pricing. As a result, the locally sourced, organic identity that Sam built over 8 years is protected. Therefore, the loan preserves what makes FreshFields special. This depends on whether Sam can afford £773/month from the £52,000 net profit (£4,333/month) while still covering personal and business expenses.

Paragraph 2 — Evaluation:

However, the loan is secured against Sam’s house. If the online expansion fails and Sam cannot make repayments, the bank could repossess the house. The investor option carries no personal risk — if the expansion fails, Sam loses nothing personally. It also depends on whether having an experienced investor on the board could actually help the business grow faster through their expertise and contacts.

Paragraph 3 — Conclusion:

Overall, I recommend Sam should take the bank loan. Giving away 40% of a profitable business making £52,000 net profit means giving away £20,800 per year in profit share — permanently. The total loan cost at 6% over 5 years is approximately £46,380 (£773 × 60), meaning the loan costs less than 3 years of shared profits. The most important factor is that the investor’s priorities may differ from Sam’s — an investor wanting returns may push for cheaper, non-organic ingredients or higher prices that conflict with FreshFields’ brand. Therefore, the bank loan is better because it preserves full ownership, costs less in the long term, and protects the brand identity Sam spent 8 years building.

questions.caseStudy: PulseGym operates 3 gyms. Revenue: £780,000/year. COGS: £234,000. Expenses: £390,000. Net profit: £156,000. Membership has been flat for 2 years. A new budget competitor charges 40% less. Option 1 — Cut costs: Reduce staffing at each gym from 8 to 5 employees (saving £108,000/year). Replace group fitness classes with self-service video screens. Close the smoothie bar (currently losing £18,000/year). Option 2 — Invest in premium services: Spend £95,000 on personal training studios, a luxury spa area and premium equipment. Increase membership price by 20%. Target high-income customers. Market research shows 35% of gym users would pay more for premium facilities.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on PulseGym’s net profit. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Cut costs:

An advantage of cutting costs is the immediate and measurable impact on net profit. Reducing staff from 8 to 5 per gym saves £108,000/year. Closing the loss-making smoothie bar saves another £18,000. Combined savings: £126,000/year. Current net profit is £156,000, so these savings would increase it to £282,000 — an 81% increase. This is because the savings go straight to the bottom line without needing to attract a single new customer. This means PulseGym’s profitability improves immediately. As a result, the business has a much stronger financial position to reinvest later. Therefore, cutting costs delivers guaranteed, immediate profit improvement. However, this depends on whether replacing group classes with video screens drives members away — many people join gyms specifically for the social experience of group classes, and the budget competitor already undercuts PulseGym on price.

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Invest in premium services:

An advantage of investing in premium services is that PulseGym differentiates itself from the budget competitor instead of competing on cost. The £95,000 investment in personal training studios, spa and premium equipment, combined with a 20% price increase, targets high-income customers. Market research shows 35% of gym users would pay more for premium facilities. This is because high-income customers are less price-sensitive and more loyal — they value quality over cost. This means PulseGym attracts a different market segment from the budget competitor, avoiding a direct price war. As a result, revenue per member increases by 20% from those willing to pay. Therefore, PulseGym creates a sustainable competitive advantage based on quality, not just lower costs. However, this depends on whether 35% of members is enough to offset the loss of members who leave because of the 20% price increase.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 2 (premium investment) will have the biggest impact on PulseGym’s net profit. Although cutting costs saves £126,000 immediately, this is outweighed by the fact that reducing staff and replacing group classes with video screens destroys the human experience that members pay for. The budget competitor already charges 40% less — PulseGym cannot win a price war, so it must compete on QUALITY. However, this depends on whether the £95,000 investment can be funded without excessive borrowing. The most important factor is that membership has been flat for 2 years — PulseGym needs to give people a reason to join (or stay), not just cut costs. In the long term, premium facilities attract loyal, high-spending members whose 20% higher fees generate recurring revenue year after year. Therefore, Option 2 will have the biggest impact because it builds long-term value through differentiation, while Option 1 risks driving members to the budget competitor.

questions.caseStudy: GreenLeaf sells organic food boxes online. Monthly revenue: £45,000. Monthly costs: £38,000. Net profit: £7,000/month. Cash flow is tight because GreenLeaf pays suppliers within 7 days but customers pay within 30 days. The business has used its £8,000 overdraft every month for 6 months. Option 1 — Negotiate longer trade credit with suppliers: Ask suppliers to extend payment terms from 7 days to 30 days. This would mean GreenLeaf receives customer payments BEFORE paying suppliers. Two of three suppliers have agreed in principle but want a 3% price increase to compensate. Option 2 — Offer customers a 5% discount for paying within 7 days: This would speed up cash inflows. Currently 60% of customers pay within 30 days and 40% pay late (45+ days). The discount would reduce revenue but improve cash flow.
questions.question: Evaluate which of these two options will have the biggest impact on GreenLeaf’s cash flow. You should consider both options before making your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Paragraph 1 — Option 1: Negotiate longer trade credit:

An advantage of extending trade credit from 7 to 30 days is that it directly addresses GreenLeaf’s core cash flow problem — paying suppliers before being paid by customers. Currently GreenLeaf pays suppliers within 7 days but customers pay within 30 days, creating a 23-day gap. Extending supplier payments to 30 days means GreenLeaf receives customer payments at roughly the same time as paying suppliers. This is because the timing of inflows and outflows would be aligned, eliminating the cash gap. This means GreenLeaf would no longer need its overdraft every month. As a result, the business saves on overdraft interest charges, which have been incurred for 6 consecutive months. Therefore, longer trade credit fixes the root cause of the cash flow problem. However, two suppliers want a 3% price increase, which would raise costs by approximately £684/month (3% of estimated monthly supplier costs).

Paragraph 2 — Option 2: Offer 5% early payment discount:

An advantage of offering a 5% early payment discount is that cash arrives 23 days faster from customers who take the discount. Currently 60% pay within 30 days and 40% pay late (45+ days). If the discount persuades most customers to pay within 7 days, GreenLeaf’s cash inflows accelerate dramatically. This is because receiving payment within 7 days rather than 30–45 days means the cash is available to pay suppliers, rent and wages on time. This means GreenLeaf may no longer need to rely on its overdraft. As a result, overdraft interest costs fall. Therefore, the discount speeds up cash inflows from the customer side. However, a 5% discount on £45,000 monthly revenue could cost up to £2,250/month if all customers take it — significantly more than the 3% supplier price increase in Option 1.

Paragraph 3 — Evaluative Conclusion:

To conclude, I think Option 1 (longer trade credit) will have the biggest impact on GreenLeaf’s cash flow. Although the early payment discount speeds up customer payments, this is outweighed by the fact that it costs up to £2,250/month (5% of £45,000 revenue) — far more than the £684/month cost of the 3% supplier price increase. The 5% discount also permanently reduces revenue on every discounted sale. However, this depends on whether the third supplier — who has not yet agreed — also accepts the extended terms. The most important factor is that GreenLeaf’s profit is only £7,000/month, so a £2,250/month discount (Option 2) would cut profit by 32%, whereas the £684/month supplier increase (Option 1) only reduces profit by 10%. In the long term, aligning payment timing with suppliers is a structural fix, while discounts are an ongoing cost. Therefore, Option 1 will have the biggest impact on cash flow because it fixes the timing mismatch at a much lower cost.
